analysis.one_liner: Creates personal Social Security investment accounts for every American, each seeded with $1,000 of federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a personal investment account for every person with a Social Security number, seeded with $1,000 from the federal Treasury — money raised by selling off federal assets. Workers could add up to $7,000 a year, with a $2,000 tax deduction, and choose among three funds like those offered to federal employees: government securities, fixed income, or a stock index fund. Monthly Social Security checks would be paid first out of each person's account, with the traditional system covering any shortfall, and at retirement account holders could take an annuity or transfer the money. Anyone choosing the stock or fixed-income funds would sign a form acknowledging the government does not protect them from losses.
analysis.who_benefits: Every person with a Social Security number would receive a $1,000 opening balance, and anyone who saves in the account gets an above-the-line tax deduction of up to $2,000 a year that is available whether or not they itemize. The deduction is worth most to people with spare cash to contribute, and investment gains accrue tax-deferred until withdrawal. Retirees could convert their balance into annuities or roll it into other retirement plans.

how_it_helps.text: Every living Social Security number holder gets an investment account with a $1,000 initial balance transferred from the Treasury, financed by receipts from federal asset sales.

Contributors can deduct up to $2,000 per year of cash contributions to their account from gross income, even without itemizing, and balances up to $7,000 in annual contributions grow with allocated earnings.

Account holders choose among a government securities fund, a fixed income fund, and a stock index fund modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan for federal employees, with semiannual elections and periodic statements evaluating each option.

At retirement, holders can take an annuity, deferred annuity, substantially equal payments, or transfer the balance to another eligible retirement plan, and the balance passes to heirs as a death distribution (except the original $1,000 federal seed, which returns to the Treasury).

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury funds the $1,000-per-person seed accounts out of receipts from selling federal assets, with a fast-track procedure letting the President propose further asset sales that Congress must vote on within 120 days. Workers who pick the fixed income or stock funds bear the investment risk themselves — the bill requires them to acknowledge the government does not protect them from losses. Monthly Social Security benefits would be drawn out of each person's account balance first, reducing the balance otherwise available as an annuity or inheritance.

drawbacks.text: Account holders who choose the fixed income or stock index funds must sign an acknowledgement that the investment is at their own risk and that returns are not guaranteed by the government.
The $2,000 annual tax deduction only helps people who have cash to contribute, so lower-income workers would get the $1,000 seed but little of the tax benefit that accrues to savers.

The $1,000 seed money comes from sales of federal assets, and the bill builds an expedited procedure that strips away amendments, points of order, and committee discretion so Congress must vote up or down on presidential recommendations for further asset sales within 120 days.

Monthly insurance benefits are paid out of each account holder's investment account first, so the account balance that could otherwise become an annuity or death benefit is depleted by ordinary benefit payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real, tangible asset — a $1,000 seed and a new tax-advantaged savings vehicle — to every Social Security number holder. But the design has a regressive core: the tax deduction flows to those who already have money to save, the seed financing depends on unspecified federal asset sales with a procedure designed to force those sales through quickly, and savers who take market risk do so with no government backstop. The bill also never resolved how accounts would interact with the existing benefit formula over time. It received no committee scrutiny, so none of these questions was ever worked out.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late September 1996 with no cosponsors, it was referred to three committees but never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Petri introduced the bill on September 26, 1996, near the end of the 104th Congress.
It was referred to the Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, and Rules committees, none of which took further action.
The only action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on September 28, 1996.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died untouched, Social Security's existing benefit structure stayed in place and no new mandated market for insurers or asset managers was created. Supporters of personal accounts gained nothing, but neither did any retiree face the bill's investment-risk shift.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Guaranteed Social Security stayed exactly as it was

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks in the Congressional Record, and attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill.

against.name: House Government Reform and Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no roll-call record exists; the lone sponsor was a Republican and no members of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: At retirement, the Executive Director must spend each account holder's balance to purchase an annuity contract from an entity in the business of selling annuities, with bonding and contract protections required. This creates a large, mandatory stream of annuity customers for insurers, though the government acts as the buyer on annuitants' behalf. Sources: S3.

industries.industry: Asset managers and financial services firms
industries.note: The fixed income fund invests in insurance contracts, certificates of deposit, and other instruments selected by qualified professional asset managers, and the stock index fund requires a replicated portfolio. Every American's account would be permanently channeled into these managed products, though the federal board keeps costs low and bars voting rights. Sources: S3.

industries.industry: Bank issuers of certificates of deposit
industries.note: Certificates of deposit are named as an eligible fixed income investment, so bank deposit products gain a large mandated buyer. Sources: S3.

The $1,000 per-account seed would come from the federal share of receipts under payment laws, and the bill's fast-track mechanism pushes further sales of federal assets to keep the program funded — an ongoing supply of government property to prospective buyers. Sources: S3.
